record.paper_title: On Some Open Problems in Monotonic and Conservative Learning
record.context_brief: strong monotonicity versus iterative informant learning
record.original_question: Does there exist an indexed family of languages over the natural numbers, meaning a class of languages for which membership in each language can be effectively decided from its index, with the following separation property for learning from informants? An informant supplies membership information for every natural number, and a learner succeeds when its sequence of indices for languages stabilizes to a correct index for the target language. A learner is strongly monotonic when the languages denoted by its later conjectures always contain the languages denoted by its earlier conjectures. An iterative learner is one whose next conjecture depends only on its previous conjecture and the latest datum. Is there such an indexed family that is strongly monotonically identifiable from informant by some algorithmic learner, but is not strongly monotonically identifiable from informant by any iterative learner, even when the iterative learner may choose its hypothesis space? A stronger positive form asks for the successful learner to use a class-preserving hypothesis space, so that its hypotheses denote only languages from the learned class.

evidence.quote: Lange and Zeugmann [LZ92] asked whether there exists an indexed family which can be strongly monotonically identified by a learner from informant, but which cannot be strongly monotonically identified by an iterative learner from informant.

We show that there exists an indexed family which can be strongly monotonically identified using a class preserving hypothesis space but cannot be strongly monotonically identified by an iterative learner, even if the iterative learner is free in the choice of the hypothesis space used.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{N}$ denote the natural numbers. An indexed family of languages is a sequence $(L_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ of subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ together with a total recursive function $f : \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \{0,1\}$ such that $f(i,x) = 1$ iff $x \in L_i$.

An informant for a language $L \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is an infinite sequence enumerating every pair $(x, \chi_L(x))$ for $x \in \mathbb{N}$, where $\chi_L$ is the characteristic function of $L$. A learner $M$ is a (possibly partial) computable function that, given a finite initial segment of an informant, outputs an index (in some hypothesis space, i.e., an effective numbering of languages). $M$ identifies $L$ in the limit from informants if, on every informant for $L$, the sequence of conjectured indices converges to a single index that denotes $L$.

The learner $M$ is strongly monotonic if, for every informant and any two stages $n < m$, the language denoted by its conjecture at stage $n$ is a subset of the language denoted by its conjecture at stage $m$. The learner is iterative if there is a computable function $F$ and an initial conjecture $h_0$ such that the conjecture at stage $n+1$ depends only on the previous conjecture $h_n$ and the next datum from the informant: $h_{n+1} = F(h_n, d_{n+1})$.

A hypothesis space $(H_j)_{j \in \mathbb{N}}$ used by a learner for an indexed family $(L_i)$ is called class-preserving if every $H_j$ equals some $L_i$.

Question: Does there exist an indexed family $(L_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that
(a) $(L_i)$ is strongly monotonically identifiable in the limit from informants by some algorithmic learner (using a class-preserving hypothesis space), yet
(b) $(L_i)$ is not strongly monotonically identifiable in the limit from informants by any iterative learner, regardless of the hypothesis space the iterative learner is permitted to use?
artifact.status_search_result: The question, originally posed by Lange and Zeugmann, has been answered affirmatively: there exists an indexed family which is strongly monotonically identifiable from informant by a learner using a class-preserving hypothesis space, but not by any iterative learner even with an arbitrary hypothesis space. This separation is established in recent work on incremental learning in the limit from positive and negative information.

status_evidence.title: Towards a Map for Incremental Learning in the Limit from Positive and Negative Information
status_evidence.snippet: Map of incremental (iterative) learning from informant including strong-monotonic learning, resolving open problems of Lange and Zeugmann.
status_evidence.claim: Separation between strong-monotonic learning from informant and its iterative version for indexed families is established.
